svg.aria-label: Diagram: how long IAM access changes take to propagate when made by editing a policy versus by changing group membership, why the recommended unit of access is the slowest to revoke, the four group types and the rules against mixing or nesting them, and two concrete gaps involving domain-restricted sharing and enforcement group membership
svg.title: Google Groups as the unit of access: the right unit, and the slowest one to revoke
svg.text: Groups are the recommended unit of access. They are also the slowest to revoke.
Editing the policy directly takes minutes. Removing somebody from a group can take hours or longer.
How long an access change takes to take effect
How you make the change
Typically
Potentially
Edit the allow or deny policy directly
2 minutes
7 minutes or longer
Change a group membership
several minutes
HOURS or longer
Change a nested group membership
several minutes
HOURS or longer
Adding propagates FASTER than removing. Groups propagate faster than nested groups.
So the direction you care about most is the slow one
Access changes are eventually consistent: principals might still use a recently revoked role.
The emergency case — get this person out now — is the case groups are worst at.
And an external IdP stacks on top: up to several hours for a change to reach the access group.
Direct policy edit stays the break-glass path. Groups are for steady state, not for incidents.
Four group types, and the pitfall is mixing them
ORGANIZATIONAL (HR-sourced) · COLLABORATION (ad hoc) · ACCESS (grants) · ENFORCEMENT (restricts)
Org groups may be members of the others. Never the reverse. Avoid granting access to org groups:
all users in an organizational group rarely need the same level of access.
Do not nest access groups or enforcement groups: nesting hides who has access, and why.
Two gaps worth knowing about
1. DRS applies to GROUPS but not to group MEMBERS. An access group allowing external members
is a loophole that undermines domain-restricted sharing.
2. Enforcement groups carry 2SV and SAML profile assignment, and by default users can LEAVE.
Set whoCanLeaveGroup to NONE_CAN_LEAVE, or the MFA from #51 becomes opt-out.
Auditing it is licence-gated: transitive membership queries need Enterprise Standard or Plus, or
Cloud Identity Premium — and the query FAILS on a nested group owned by another organization.
#48 an author you cannot see. #49 a referent you cannot name. #50 deletable by a query shape.
#51 a documented exemption. #52 the right unit of access, revoking in minutes to hours.
